title: Tilenus: posse non mori is of nature, non posse mori of glory
source_text: XXII. Tilenus quoque Disputatione de statu externo primi hominis thesi nona. Sciendum est, inquit, immortalitatem primi hominis non plane ejusdem fuisse rationis cum gloriosa Beatorum immortalitate. Nam ut aliud est posse non peccare, & non posse peccare: sic aliud posse non mori, & non posse mori. Illud est naturae, hoc gloriae. Prior immortalitas moriendi actum tollit, potestatem non excludit: posterior utrumque abolet & extinguit.
pass_a_gloss: Tilenus also in the Disputation on the external state of the first man, ninth thesis. It must be known, he says, that the immortality of the first man was not plainly of the same character as the glorious immortality of the Blessed. For as it is one thing to be able not to sin, and not to be able to sin: so it is one thing to be able not to die, and not to be able to die. That is of nature, this of glory. The former immortality takes away the act of dying, does not exclude the power: the latter abolishes and extinguishes both.
pass_b_english: Tilenus says the same in his Disputation on the External State of the First Man, ninth thesis: "It should be understood that the first man's immortality was not wholly of the same kind as the glorious immortality of the blessed. For as being able not to sin is one thing and being unable to sin another, so being able not to die is one thing and being unable to die another. The first belongs to nature, the second to glory. The first kind of immortality removes the act of dying but does not rule out the power to die; the second abolishes and extinguishes both."

lemmas.gloss: not wholly of the same kind

choices.english: The first belongs to nature, the second to glory
choices.why: Illud/hoc refer back to the two powers just named; the English makes the order explicit.
